paragraphs.title: Jerusalem Loses Her Status and Becomes Desolate

easy.explanation: She sits alone, like a widow.
easy.q: How does the city sit at the beginning of the lament?

easy.explanation: The ways of Zion mourn because none come to the solemn feasts.
easy.q: What has happened to the ways of Zion?
Who sighs among the people of the city?

answers: She has changed from a great ruling city into a solitary tributary city
She has changed from a village into a capital
She has changed from a desolate city into a crowded city
medium.explanation: She was great among nations but has become solitary and tributary.
medium.q: What major change has occurred in Jerusalem’s status?

answers: Subject to another power and required to pay tribute
medium.explanation: A tributary city is under another power and owes tribute.
medium.q: What does “tributary” mean in the description of Jerusalem?

answers: They show that every part of city life is grieving
medium.explanation: The priests sigh and the virgins are afflicted.
medium.q: How do the priests and virgins reinforce the picture of Jerusalem’s ruin?

answers: Loneliness and loss of former standing
challenge.explanation: The widow image conveys isolation and loss.
challenge.q: What does the comparison to a widow emphasize?

answers: They prove that new construction has begun
Their emptiness shows that normal city life has stopped
They describe the borders of the kingdom
challenge.explanation: Normally roads and gates are busy, but here they are mournful and desolate.
challenge.q: Why are the roads and gates important details in this description?

answers: They focus only on military strength
The people’s condition contradicts the city’s condition
The people’s grief gives human expression to the city’s desolation
challenge.explanation: The sighing priests and afflicted virgins embody the city’s sorrow.
challenge.q: How do verses 1–4 connect the city’s condition with that of its people?

paragraphs.title: Enemies Exploit the Ruin and the People Go into Exile

easy.explanation: Her adversaries are the chief, and her enemies prosper.
Her children have gone into captivity before the enemy.

answers: Her pleasant things from the days of old
easy.explanation: She remembered the pleasant things she had in former days.
easy.q: What did Jerusalem remember in her affliction?

answers: The LORD afflicted her because of the multitude of her transgressions
The passage does not connect sin and suffering
medium.explanation: The text directly says the LORD afflicted her for her transgressions.
medium.q: According to the passage, how are Jerusalem’s transgressions related to her suffering?

medium.explanation: Affliction refers to suffering and hardship.
medium.q: What does “affliction” mean in this passage?

answers: They lead the people with strength
They sit safely in the palace
They are like deer without pasture and have no strength
medium.explanation: They become like harts that find no pasture and flee without strength.

answers: The ruin affects both leaders and the wider population
challenge.explanation: The princes are powerless and the children are taken captive.
challenge.q: What does the movement from the princes to the children reveal?

answers: It highlights the contrast between former prosperity and present ruin
It proves that the enemies have departed
challenge.explanation: Past blessings make the present devastation more painful.
challenge.q: Why does remembering former pleasant things increase Jerusalem’s sorrow?

answers: They intend to help her worship
They rejoice in her downfall and despise her sacred observances
challenge.explanation: The adversaries saw her condition and mocked her sabbaths.
challenge.q: What does the enemies’ mocking of Jerusalem’s sabbaths show?

easy.explanation: Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she is removed.
easy.q: What is presented as the reason Jerusalem was removed?

easy.explanation: The heathen entered into her sanctuary.

answers: To obtain meat and relieve their souls
easy.explanation: They exchanged their pleasant things for food.
easy.q: Why did the people give away their pleasant things?

answers: Her nakedness is seen, and those who honored her despise her
She receives greater honor than before
medium.explanation: Those who honored her despise her after seeing her nakedness.
medium.q: How is Jerusalem humiliated before the nations?

answers: Rejected and taken from her former position
medium.explanation: Jerusalem has been rejected and brought down.
medium.q: What does “removed” mean in this context?

answers: Both show an assault on her holiness and dignity
medium.explanation: Her nakedness and violated sanctuary express humiliation.
medium.q: How are the exposure of Jerusalem and the heathen entering the sanctuary related?

answers: She failed to consider the consequences of her actions
challenge.explanation: She did not consider where her conduct would finally lead.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from “she remembereth not her last end”?

answers: The people surrendered what was precious to obtain nourishment
The enemy freely supplied their food
challenge.explanation: Giving up valued possessions for food shows extreme need.
challenge.q: Why does exchanging pleasant things for food emphasize the severity of the famine?

answers: They defend her after seeing it
They despise and humiliate her because they see it
challenge.explanation: Her exposed condition leads those who honored her to despise her.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between Jerusalem’s nakedness and the response of those who honored her?

paragraphs.title: Jerusalem Appeals to Passersby and Describes Her Suffering

easy.explanation: She addresses all who pass by.
easy.q: To whom does Jerusalem speak when asking them to look at her sorrow?

easy.explanation: Fire was sent from above into her bones.
easy.q: What image describes the suffering sent upon her?

answers: They were crushed and trodden down
easy.explanation: The Lord trod down the mighty men and crushed the young men.
easy.q: What happened to her mighty men and young men?

answers: Look and see whether any sorrow is like her sorrow
medium.explanation: She asks them to behold and compare her sorrow.
medium.q: What does Jerusalem ask passersby to do?

medium.explanation: To be desolate is to be left ruined and empty.

answers: They describe a journey of victory
They portray pain, entrapment, and heavy oppression
medium.explanation: The images show suffering that burns, traps, and weighs down.
medium.q: How do the images of fire, a net, and a yoke work together?

answers: It makes her suffering a public witness for everyone who sees her
It hides her suffering from the people
It changes the scene into a public celebration
challenge.explanation: She asks every traveler to recognize the extraordinary depth of her pain.
challenge.q: Why does Jerusalem’s appeal to passersby intensify the lament?

answers: The transgressions are pictured as a heavy burden
challenge.explanation: Her sins are represented as a yoke bound around her neck.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “The yoke of my transgressions” teach about sin and suffering?

answers: They are preparing for a feast
They are being appointed as leaders
They are being crushed and trampled
challenge.explanation: Being trodden like grapes represents violent defeat and destruction.
challenge.q: What does the winepress image communicate about Judah’s young men?

paragraphs.title: Weeping, Surrender, and Acceptance of Judgment

easy.explanation: He says, “For these things I weep.”
easy.q: What does the speaker do because of these things?

easy.explanation: Her children are desolate because the enemy prevailed.
easy.q: What has happened to Jerusalem’s children?
What does Jerusalem say about the LORD?

answers: The comforter is far away and the children are desolate
medium.explanation: The comforter is absent and the enemy has prevailed over her children.
The image conveys rejection and uncleanness among the nations.
medium.q: What does “as a menstruous woman” communicate in this passage?

answers: She acknowledges the LORD’s righteousness and her rebellion
medium.explanation: She says the LORD is righteous because she rebelled against his commandment.
medium.q: How does Jerusalem respond to her condition?

answers: Those who might have helped are dead, absent, or deceitful
The leaders remain untouched by the famine
challenge.explanation: The priests and elders die seeking food, while her lovers deceive her.
challenge.q: How does “there is none to comfort her” relate to the priests, elders, and allies?

answers: She admits that she disobeyed the LORD
She asks for judgment to be canceled
challenge.explanation: The statement is an acknowledgment of rebellion.
challenge.q: What does “I have rebelled against his commandment” reveal about Jerusalem’s position?

answers: They deceived her when she called for help
challenge.explanation: She called for her lovers, but they deceived her.
challenge.q: How are Jerusalem’s allies shown to have failed her?

paragraphs.title: A Plea before God and a Request for Retribution

easy.explanation: The speaker repeatedly calls upon the LORD.
easy.q: To whom does the speaker appeal?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “abroad the sword bereaveth.”

answers: That their wickedness come before God and they be dealt with as Jerusalem was
easy.explanation: He asks God to bring their wickedness before him and judge them.
easy.q: What does the speaker ask to happen to the enemies?

answers: His bowels are troubled and his heart is turned within him
medium.explanation: The language describes intense bodily and emotional distress.
medium.q: How is the speaker’s physical and inward condition described?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes severe inward distress.
medium.q: What does “my bowels are troubled” express?

answers: Safety exists both outside and inside
Death and danger surround people both outside and inside
medium.explanation: The sword is outside, while death-like suffering is inside.
medium.q: What contrast appears in “abroad the sword bereaveth, at home there is as death”?

answers: He attributes the judgment to the LORD
He says everything happened by chance
challenge.explanation: He recognizes that the LORD has brought the appointed day.
challenge.q: What does “thou hast done it” show about the speaker’s view of events?

answers: It asks that the suffering be forgotten
It asks that the enemies experience comparable trouble
It asks that the enemies receive authority
challenge.explanation: The speaker asks God to do to them as he has done to Jerusalem.
challenge.q: How is the request for retribution connected with the earlier suffering?

answers: A request that the enemies escape pain
A request that the enemies become rulers
A request that the enemies experience the speaker’s grievous condition
challenge.explanation: The speaker asks that the enemies share his suffering.
challenge.q: What does “they shall be like unto me” add to the prayer?
